I am 38 years old and have been farming since I was a teenager. My family has about 8 mu of good flat land here in Quzhou. I did not go far in school, but I know this land and this climate. Every year I do the same thing my father did and what my neighbors do, because it works.

This year I will grow winter wheat and summer maize on the same 8 mu, just like always. This is the only system I trust. If I tried cotton or vegetables, I might lose everything — I don't have the money to take that risk, and I don't know those markets. Wheat and maize have buyers who come right to the village, and the government gives us a small subsidy for wheat. I need that steady income to feed my family and pay for my children's school.

For wheat, I will plant **Jimai 22** in early October. It is a good improved variety that my neighbors have used for years — it stands up well and gives about 1000 jin per mu if the weather is normal. Before planting, I will do **rotary tillage** to prepare the seedbed. I will put down 100 jin of compound fertilizer as a basal dressing and topdress with urea in the spring. Wheat needs a lot of water, so I will irrigate four times: winter irrigation to protect from freezing, and three more times in spring when the grain is filling. I will spray pesticides four times — herbicide once, and then insecticide and fungicide two or three times because the aphids and rust always come.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant **Denghai 605** maize with **no-tillage**. There is no time to waste between crops — only about ten days. Denghai 605 is a hybrid that gives good yield, usually around 1100 jin per mu. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and maybe some urea at the jointing stage. Maize needs less water than wheat, so I will irrigate twice — once when it is young and once during flowering. I will spray pesticides three times: herbicide at the start, then insecticide for the corn borer, and fungicide if it looks necessary.

I use these amounts of fertilizer because that is what the seed shop recommends and what I have always done. I would rather use a little too much than too little — if I under-fertilize and the yield drops, my family suffers. The government technician came once and said we could use less nitrogen, but I don't trust that. My neighbor cut back two years ago and his wheat was shorter than mine.
